question: Which statement best describes Choose a source?
options: Choose local or hosted font files deliberately. Local files can provide control and avoid a third-party request; hosted services may offer a broad library. Review licensing, privacy, and loading behavior. Consider the user’s connection as well as the brand when selecting a source. Local and hosted sources have different licensing, privacy, caching, and deployment considerations. Choose a source the team can legally and reliably serve. A font source is like choosing between supplies kept in-house and a delivery service.

A fallback stack gives the browser another font if the preferred one cannot load. Choose a fallback with similar proportions so text remains readable and layout changes are smaller. For example, set a system sans-serif fallback after the preferred family. Test the fallback state, not only the final font. Fallback fonts should support the page’s language and special characters. Compare their widths with the preferred font to limit content shifts. A fallback font is like a backup speaker who can still deliver the message.

Font display behavior controls what users see while a font downloads. Showing fallback text immediately keeps content available; hiding text can make the page appear blank. Test on a slow connection and watch for layout shifts when the custom font replaces the fallback. Readable text should appear while a font loads. Measure layout shift and test on a slow connection, rather than judging only the final screenshot. Showing fallback text is like putting up a temporary sign while the final one is printed.

Include only the font weights and character subsets the design needs. Extra files increase downloads. For example, if the page uses regular and bold only, avoid loading several unused weights. Check that each file actually provides the requested weight instead of relying on synthetic bold. Variable font files can provide several weights in one file, but still have a size cost. Include only the ranges and subsets the design uses. Loading only used weights is like packing only the tools needed for the job.
